name: REST API
explanation: An HTTP interface where clients read and change resources using methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
triggers: api;backend;get data from the server;send data to the server;fetch data
requirements: Use nouns for resources and HTTP methods for actions, such as GET /orders;Return correct status codes, such as 201 created, 400 bad input and 404 not found;Validate every input and return errors in one consistent format;Paginate list endpoints;Version the API, so changes do not break existing clients;Accept only allowed fields when creating or updating records, to prevent mass assignment;Use plural nouns in paths, and POST to a sub-path such as /orders/{id}:cancel for actions that are not CRUD;Never return passwords or stored secrets, and show a new API key only once, when it is created
done_when: Every endpoint is documented with its inputs, outputs and errors;Invalid input gets a clear 4xx error, never a 500;An OpenAPI description with title, version and contact is published and matches the deployed API

name: Rate limiting
explanation: Capping how many requests a client can make in a time window, to protect a service from abuse or overload.
triggers: too many requests;spam;abuse;limit requests;block bots;per minute;hammering;brute force;too many attempts;login attempts
requirements: Limit requests per user, API key or IP address in a time window;Apply stricter limits to login, sign-up and password reset;Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header;Enforce limits on the server or gateway, shared across all instances;Limit request body size, uploads and expensive queries
done_when: Going over the limit returns 429 and blocks further requests for a while;Normal use never hits the limit

name: CORS
explanation: Cross-origin resource sharing: browser rules and server headers that control which websites are allowed to call an API.
triggers: cors error;blocked by the browser;different domain;another domain;frontend and backend on different ports
requirements: Allow only the specific origins that need access, never * together with credentials;Never copy the request's Origin into the response without checking it against a list;Allow only the methods and headers that are needed;Remember CORS is not access control, and check authentication on the server too;Check the origin of postMessage events, and send messages to a specific origin, never *
done_when: Allowed origins can read responses, and the browser blocks other origins from reading them;No response allows every origin while also allowing credentials

name: API keys and tokens
explanation: Protecting an API so only allowed apps or users can call it, using API keys, bearer tokens such as JWTs, or OAuth access tokens.
triggers: protect the api;secure the api;who can call;only my app;token expires
requirements: Send tokens in the Authorization header over HTTPS, never in URLs;Store API keys hashed, and let users revoke and rotate them;Give access tokens a short lifetime, and use refresh tokens;Verify JWT signatures with an allowlist of algorithms, and never accept none;Give each key only the permissions it needs
done_when: Requests with missing, expired or revoked credentials get 401;A key with a limited scope cannot call other endpoints

name: Webhooks
explanation: HTTP requests that another service sends to your server when something happens, such as a payment succeeding, so you don't have to keep asking.
triggers: notify my server;tell my app when;call my api when;payment succeeds;listen for events
requirements: Verify the signature of every incoming webhook with the sender's secret;Reply quickly with a 2xx status, and do the work in a background job;Handle duplicate deliveries using the event id;Handle events that arrive out of order;Reject old events by checking their timestamp;Compare signatures with a constant-time comparison
done_when: A request with a wrong signature is rejected;The same event delivered twice has the effect of one

name: GraphQL API
explanation: An API where clients ask for exactly the data they need in one query, described by a typed schema.
requirements: Check authorization in every resolver, not only at the endpoint;Limit query depth, complexity and the number of items returned;Turn off introspection and detailed errors in production unless you need them;Validate arguments with the schema and with your own rules;Batch database calls with a loader to avoid one query per item;Rate-limit by query cost, not only by the number of requests
done_when: A very deep or very large query is rejected;No field lets a user read another user's data

name: API error responses
explanation: Returning errors from an API in one consistent, machine-readable format, such as Problem Details (RFC 9457).
triggers: api errors;error messages from the api;return an error;error codes;validation errors in the api;consistent errors;error format;returns errors;error shape;error response;errors from the api
requirements: Return errors as Problem Details JSON (application/problem+json) with type, title, status and detail;Use the right status code: 4xx for client mistakes, 5xx for server faults;List field validation errors with the field name and what is wrong;Give each error a stable type or code that clients can rely on;Never expose stack traces, SQL or other internal details in error responses;Include a request id so a reported error can be found in the logs
done_when: Every error from the API has the same shape and a correct status code;Clients can tell error types apart without reading the message text

name: Filtering and sorting in APIs
explanation: Letting API clients ask for part of a collection, in a chosen order, with only the fields they need.
triggers: filter the results;sort the results;only return some fields;api query parameters;search parameters;order the list by;sort and filter;filter and sort;filter the list
requirements: Support filtering with documented, validated query parameters;Allow sorting only on indexed fields, and document the default order;Let clients request only the fields they need, such as fields=id,name;Reject unknown filter or sort fields with a clear 400 error instead of ignoring them;Combine filters with pagination so results stay consistent between pages;Never build database queries by pasting filter values into strings
done_when: Filtering and sorting return correct results across all pages;Unsupported filters are rejected with a clear error

name: API versioning and deprecation
explanation: Changing an API without breaking existing clients, and retiring old versions with clear notice.
triggers: change the api without breaking;old clients;deprecate an endpoint;remove an old endpoint;v2 of the api;new version of the api
requirements: Make only backward-compatible changes within a version, such as adding optional fields;Treat removing or renaming fields, and changing types or meanings, as breaking changes;Make clients ignore unknown response fields, and make servers reject unknown request fields with 400;Put the major version in the URL or a header, and keep old versions running for a stated time;Announce deprecations in the documentation and with Deprecation and Sunset headers;Check who still calls a deprecated endpoint before removing it
done_when: Existing clients keep working after every non-breaking release;Clients of a deprecated endpoint get notice and a date before it is removed

name: Safe retries (idempotency)
explanation: Making sure a request that is sent again, after a timeout or retry, has the same effect as sending it once.
triggers: double submit;charged twice;duplicate orders;retry safely;request sent twice;same request twice;created twice
requirements: Accept an Idempotency-Key header, or request id, on POST requests that create or charge something;Store the key before processing, return 409 Conflict while the first request is still running, then replay the saved result;Reject a reused key that comes with a different request body;Keep keys long enough to cover client retries, such as 24 hours;Make PUT and DELETE idempotent by design
done_when: Sending the same create request twice with one key creates one record;A retried payment never charges twice

name: Long-running API operations
explanation: API calls that start work taking longer than one request should, and let the client check on it later.
triggers: takes minutes;check progress later;status endpoint;request times out;report when it is done;long task in the api;times out;several minutes;takes too long to respond
requirements: Return 202 Accepted with a link to an operation status resource;Report status (running, succeeded or failed), progress, and the result or error in that resource;Tell clients how often to poll with Retry-After, or notify them with a webhook;Let clients cancel an operation where possible;Make starting the operation safe to repeat with an idempotency key;Keep finished results for a stated time
done_when: A client can start the work, poll its status, and get the result or the error;Long work never fails because of an HTTP timeout

name: Conditional requests (ETags)
explanation: Using ETags so clients skip downloading unchanged data, and so two people cannot overwrite each other's changes.
triggers: lost update;edit at the same time;overwrite each other;only download if changed;concurrent edits;someone else changed it;loses their changes;lose their changes;edit the same
requirements: Return an ETag, or version number, with each resource;Answer If-None-Match with 304 Not Modified when nothing changed;Require If-Match on updates and deletes, and return 412 Precondition Failed when the resource changed;Change the ETag whenever the resource changes, including changes by other users;Tell users clearly when their edit conflicts, and let them see the newer version
done_when: Two people saving the same record can never silently overwrite each other;Unchanged resources are not downloaded again

name: Batch API operations
explanation: Creating, updating or deleting many items in one API request instead of one request for each.
triggers: update many at once;delete many items;bulk edit;many requests at once;select all and delete;in one call;in one request;hundreds of
requirements: Limit how many items one batch may contain, and document the limit;Decide and document whether a batch is all or nothing, or reports a result per item;Return a result for every item, in the same order, with errors per item;Check permissions for every item, not just the first;Make batches safe to retry with an idempotency key;For delete by filter, return a dry-run count first, and delete only with an explicit force flag
done_when: A batch with some invalid items reports exactly which ones failed;A batch can never touch items the user may not access

name: API data formats
explanation: Consistent formats for dates, money, quantities, enums, names and text in API requests and responses.
triggers: dates in the api;currency in json;time zone in the api;field names in json;represent money;amounts in the api;camelcase or snake_case;dates and prices;in json;send dates
requirements: Send timestamps as RFC 3339 strings in UTC, such as 2026-05-01T12:00:00Z;Send money as an exact amount, a decimal string or whole minor units, with an ISO 4217 currency code;Use one naming style for fields everywhere, such as camelCase or snake_case;Put units in quantity field names, such as size_bytes, or use ISO 8601 durations;Treat enums as extensible, so clients cope with values they do not know yet;Use UTF-8 everywhere, and say whether lengths count characters or bytes;Do not give null and a missing field different meanings unless documented;Use standard codes: ISO 3166 countries, BCP 47 languages, ISO 4217 currencies, IANA media types
done_when: Dates and amounts round-trip between client and server without loss or time zone shifts;A new enum value does not break existing clients
